queries.query: Why does my espresso taste bitter?

documents.title: Bitter espresso: the five usual causes
documents.text:
Bitter espresso almost always comes down to one of five causes: a grind that is too fine, a shot that runs too long, water that is too hot, a very dark roast, or a dirty machine. Each one pushes the shot toward over extraction, which is when the water pulls out the harsh, woody compounds that sit at the end of the extraction curve.

## How over extraction works

Coffee dissolves in stages. Acids come out first, then sugars and the heavier aromatics, and the bitter compounds come out last. A balanced shot dissolves roughly 18 to 22 percent of the coffee's mass. Above about 22 percent, most people start to taste bitterness and a dry, astringent finish.

## The five causes at a glance

| Cause | What you notice | First fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grind too fine | Shot runs slow, over 35 seconds | Go one step coarser |
| Shot too long | Pale, watery stream at the end | Stop at a 1:2 ratio |
| Water too hot | Harsh edge even on good beans | Drop 2 °C |
| Very dark roast | Smoky, ashy taste | Try a medium roast |
| Dirty machine | Rancid, stale bitterness | Backflush and scrub the basket |

## Which cause is most likely?

In a set of 60 home shots we logged over two weeks, grind size explained the most variation in taste. Shots that ran longer than 35 seconds were rated bitter 71 percent of the time, while shots between 25 and 30 seconds were rated bitter only 18 percent of the time. Temperature mattered less, but it still showed up: shots pulled at 96 °C were rated bitter about twice as often as shots at 92 °C with the same beans.

## A quick diagnostic

Taste the shot and look at how it ran. If it was slow and bitter, start with grind. If it was fast and still bitter, look at the roast and the water temperature. If every shot tastes bitter no matter what you change, clean the machine before anything else, because old coffee oils turn rancid and flavor every cup.

Change one variable at a time and write down what you changed. Two changes at once make it impossible to tell which one helped.

## Bitterness that is not over extraction

Not every bitter shot is over extracted. Three other things can taste similar:

- **Astringency.** A dry, puckering feeling on the tongue, often from channeling or from very fine particles. It feels bitter but is really a texture.
- **Roast bitterness.** Dark roasts contain bitter compounds created in the roaster. You cannot extract your way out of them.
- **Stale oils.** Coffee oils left in the basket or shower screen go rancid within a day or two and add a sharp, stale taste.

If your shot is quick, the extraction is probably not the cause, so look at these three first.

## How long it takes to fix

Most home baristas who follow a one-variable-at-a-time routine get a coffee from bitter to balanced in about five shots. In our log, the median was four shots, and only 1 in 10 coffees needed more than eight. Expect a new bag of the same coffee to need one or two small grind changes, because beans change as they age.

documents.title: Why is my coffee bitter?
documents.text:
Lots of people ask why their espresso is bitter. There are many reasons. It could be the beans, the grinder, the machine, or the water. Coffee is complicated and every setup is different, so it is hard to say for sure without tasting it.

Some beans are just bitter. Dark roasts tend to be more bitter than light roasts. Robusta beans are more bitter than arabica beans. If you buy cheap coffee from the supermarket it might be old, and old coffee can taste bitter and flat.

The grinder is also important. A good grinder makes even particles. A cheap grinder makes a mix of big and small pieces, and the small pieces can over extract and make the coffee bitter. Some people say the grinder is more important than the machine.

The machine matters too. Some machines run hot. Some machines are dirty inside. You should clean your machine regularly. Check the manual for how to clean it.

Water can make a difference. Very hard water can make coffee taste chalky, and very soft water can make it taste flat. Some people use filtered water.

You can also try adding milk or sugar if you do not like the bitter taste. A latte or a cappuccino is less bitter than a straight espresso because the milk softens it. Some people like a little bitterness, and that is fine too. Coffee is a personal thing.

In the end, the best thing to do is experiment until you find what you like. Try different beans, try different grind settings, and keep tasting. Over time you will learn what makes your coffee taste good. Happy brewing!

documents.title: Over extraction, explained for home baristas
documents.text:
When people say an espresso is bitter, they usually mean it is over extracted. Extraction is the share of the ground coffee that ends up dissolved in your cup, and it happens in a predictable order.

The first compounds to dissolve are the bright acids. They give a shot its fruit and its sparkle. Next come the sugars and the browning products from roasting, which carry sweetness and body. Last come the larger, slower molecules, many of them bitter or drying. If you stop the shot while sugars are still coming out, it tastes balanced. If you keep going, the bitter end of the curve takes over.

Anything that speeds up extraction or lets it run longer can tip a shot into bitterness:

- a finer grind, which exposes more surface area
- a higher dose of water for the same coffee, which keeps the extraction going
- hotter water, which dissolves everything faster
- a longer contact time, from a slow shot or a long pre-infusion

There is a second, sneakier cause called channeling. When the puck has a weak spot, water rushes through it. The coffee along that channel is stripped of everything, bitter compounds included, while the rest of the puck is barely touched. The result tastes bitter and sour at once, which confuses a lot of people. If your shots taste both harsh and thin, channeling is the first thing to suspect. Distributing the grounds evenly before tamping, and tamping level, fixes most of it.

Finally, remember that some bitterness is part of the style. A dark roast will taste bitter even when it is extracted perfectly, because roasting creates bitter compounds of its own. If you dislike that flavor, change the beans, not the recipe.

A useful way to picture all this is a hill. On one side of the peak, the shot is under extracted: sour, salty and thin. On the other side, it is over extracted: bitter, dry and hollow. The peak is narrow, and every variable you control moves you up or down one side of it. Most home baristas who complain of bitterness are a little way down the far side, and a small change in one variable is enough to bring them back.

It also helps to know that taste shifts as a shot cools. Bitterness is more noticeable in a hot shot and sourness is more noticeable as it cools. Taste your espresso within a minute or two of pulling it, and taste it the same way each time, so that you are comparing like with like.

documents.title: Espresso troubleshooting FAQ
documents.text:
**My espresso is bitter. What should I check first?**
Check the shot time and the grind. If a double shot takes much longer than 30 seconds, your grind is probably too fine. Go a little coarser and pull another shot.

**My shot was fast but still bitter. Why?**
A fast shot that tastes bitter usually means channeling, a very dark roast, or water that is too hot. Look at the puck after the shot. Holes or cracks point to channeling.

**Can stale beans make espresso bitter?**
Yes. Beans that are more than a month or two past their roast date lose their aromatics, and what is left tastes flat and bitter. Buy beans with a roast date on the bag and use them within about three to five weeks of that date.

**Does the machine temperature matter?**
It does. Most espresso is brewed between 90 and 96 °C. Darker roasts usually taste better toward the low end of that range, and lighter roasts toward the high end.

**Could my machine be dirty?**
If you have never backflushed your machine or cleaned the shower screen, old oils are almost certainly adding a stale, bitter taste. Clean the basket after every session and backflush with a cleaner once a week if your machine allows it.

**Is some bitterness normal?**
A little bitterness is normal in espresso, especially with dark roasts. The goal is balance, not zero bitterness. If the bitterness lingers and dries out your mouth, the shot is probably over extracted.

**What ratio should I use?**
A common starting point is 1:2, for example 18 grams of coffee in and 36 grams of espresso out. Shorter ratios taste stronger and can taste less bitter. Longer ratios taste lighter but can pull more bitterness if the grind is fine.

documents.title: What we learned from a month of bitter shots
documents.text:
I bought my first espresso machine last spring and spent most of the first month making shots I did not want to drink. Here is what was actually wrong, in the order I found it.

The first problem was the grinder. I had been using pre-ground coffee from a bag labeled for espresso. It was ground for a different machine and it was weeks old. Every shot dripped out slowly and tasted like burnt toast. Buying whole beans and a burr grinder fixed more than half of my problem in a single morning.

The second problem was my shot length. I was letting the shot run until the cup looked full, which meant pulling 60 or 70 grams of liquid from 18 grams of coffee. The last part of a long shot is thin and bitter. When I started stopping the shot at around 36 grams, the taste changed completely. It was sweeter and heavier.

The third problem was heat. My little machine has no temperature control, and it runs hot if it sits for a while. Running a few seconds of water through the group head before each shot took the harsh edge off.

The last problem was beans. I had been buying the darkest roast in the shop because I thought espresso was supposed to be dark. Switching to a medium roast made the shots far less bitter, and I could taste chocolate and nuts instead of smoke.

If you are starting out, I would fix them in the same order: fresh beans and a real grinder, then the ratio, then the temperature, then the roast. None of it needs expensive gear, just patience and a scale.

documents.title: Bitter espresso and the chemistry behind it
documents.text:
The bitterness in coffee comes from several groups of compounds, and they do not all behave the same way. Knowing which ones you are tasting helps you choose a fix.

Caffeine is bitter, but it accounts for only a small part of the bitterness in a typical cup, roughly 10 to 15 percent by most estimates. The larger share comes from compounds formed during roasting. As beans roast, chlorogenic acids break down into lactones, which taste pleasantly bitter in a medium roast. With longer roasting, those lactones break down further into phenylindanes, which have a harsher, lingering bitterness. That is why very dark roasts taste bitter regardless of how you brew them.

Extraction adds another layer. The bitter compounds in coffee are generally larger molecules that dissolve more slowly than acids and sugars. They make up a growing share of what is extracted as the shot goes on, so the last part of a long shot carries more bitterness per gram than the first part.

Temperature speeds up the extraction of everything, but it speeds up the slow compounds most. A rise from 90 to 96 °C can noticeably increase bitterness in a dark roast while doing less harm to a light roast, which has fewer of those compounds to begin with.

Here is a simple summary:

| Source of bitterness | Where it comes from | What helps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Caffeine | The bean itself | Little you can change |
| Lactones | Medium roasting | Usually pleasant in balance |
| Phenylindanes | Dark roasting | A lighter roast |
| Late extraction | Long or slow shots | A coarser grind, a shorter ratio |

The practical lesson is that roast level sets the floor for bitterness, and extraction decides how far above that floor your shot ends up.

documents.title: Bitter, sour or astringent? A tasting guide for espresso
documents.text:
Many people call any unpleasant espresso "bitter", but bitterness, sourness and astringency come from different problems and need different fixes. Learning to tell them apart saves a lot of wasted coffee.

## Three tastes that get confused

| Taste | Where you notice it | What it feels like | Usual cause |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bitter | Back of the tongue, lingering | Heavy, like strong black tea or burnt toast | Over extraction or a dark roast |
| Sour | Sides of the tongue, quick | Sharp, like lemon juice or unripe fruit | Under extraction |
| Astringent | The whole mouth, drying | Puckering, like a strong red wine | Channeling, uneven grind, very fine particles |

The easiest test is to wait ten seconds after you swallow. Sourness fades quickly. Bitterness hangs on. Astringency leaves your mouth feeling dry and rough, as if the coffee had taken moisture away.

## A simple training exercise

Pull three shots from the same beans on purpose: one very fast (about 15 seconds), one normal (about 28 seconds) and one very slow (about 45 seconds). Taste them side by side at the same temperature. The fast shot shows you sourness, the slow one shows you bitterness, and the normal one should sit in between. In our training sessions, 9 out of 12 new home baristas could name the fast and slow shots correctly after this exercise, compared with 4 out of 12 before it.

## What to do once you know

- **If it is bitter**, grind a little coarser, stop the shot earlier, or lower the water temperature by one or two degrees.
- **If it is sour**, grind finer or let the shot run longer.
- **If it is astringent**, look at your puck preparation. Distribute the grounds evenly, tamp level, and check the spent puck for holes or cracks that show where water rushed through.

## A note on milk drinks

Milk hides sourness well but makes bitterness easier to notice in the finish, especially with dark roasts. If your straight shots taste fine but your lattes taste bitter, the milk may be overheated. Milk steamed above about 70 °C loses its sweetness, and the coffee's bitterness stands out more.

Tasting is a skill. The more shots you compare on purpose, the faster you will know which dial to turn.

documents.title: Forum thread: every shot I pull is bitter, what am I doing wrong?
documents.text:
**Original post:** I bought a home espresso machine two weeks ago and every single shot tastes bitter. I use a supermarket dark roast, 18 grams in, and I let it run until the cup looks full. I have tried tamping harder and it is still bitter. Any ideas?

**Reply 1:** How much comes out, and how long does it take? "Until the cup looks full" could be 60 grams. That is a lot for an 18 gram dose. Try stopping at about 36 grams.

**Original poster:** I never weighed it. I will try that tonight.

**Reply 2:** Also, dark supermarket roasts are bitter to start with. You can make them less bitter but you cannot make them taste like a light roast. Try a medium roast from a local roaster with a roast date on the bag.

**Reply 3:** Tamping harder does almost nothing once the coffee is compressed. Grind size changes the flow far more than tamp pressure. Keep the tamp the same and adjust the grinder instead.

**Reply 4:** Check when your machine was last cleaned. If it came with a blind basket, backflush it with plain water. Old oil in the group head tastes bitter and rancid.

**Original poster (update):** Stopping at 36 grams made a huge difference. The shot took about 27 seconds and it is much sweeter. Still a bit bitter at the end, so I will try a medium roast next week.

**Reply 5:** Nice. One more thing: drink it soon. Espresso that sits for a few minutes gets more bitter as it cools and the crema breaks down.

**Original poster (second update):** New beans arrived. With the medium roast and the same recipe, the bitterness is mostly gone. Thanks everyone. Summary for anyone who finds this thread later: weigh your output, do not overfill the cup, and do not expect dark roasts to taste sweet.

**Reply 6:** Good summary. I would add: change one thing at a time. If you change the beans and the grind on the same day you will not know which fixed it.

**Reply 7:** And write your shots down. A notebook with dose, yield, time and a one-word taste note is the cheapest upgrade you can make. After a week you will see patterns you would never notice from memory, like the beans getting faster as they age.

documents.title: 7 reasons your espresso is bitter (and one that is not your fault)
documents.text:
Bitter espresso is frustrating, but the cause is usually simple. Here are the seven most common reasons, roughly in order of how often we see them, plus one that has nothing to do with your technique.

## 1. The grind is too fine

Fine grounds slow the water down and expose more surface area, so the shot extracts too much. If your shot takes longer than 35 seconds, this is the first thing to change.

## 2. The shot runs too long

Even with the right grind, letting the shot run past a 1:2 or 1:2.5 ratio pulls out the last, harshest compounds. Weigh your output and stop on time.

## 3. The water is too hot

Most machines are set around 93 °C. Some run hotter than their display says. If everything else looks right, try lowering the temperature by two degrees.

## 4. The roast is very dark

Dark roasts are bitter by nature. You can soften them with a coarser grind, a shorter ratio and a lower temperature, but you cannot remove the roast flavor.

## 5. The machine is dirty

Coffee oils build up in the group head, shower screen and basket. After a few days they turn rancid and make every shot taste stale and bitter. Backflush and scrub regularly.

## 6. The beans are stale

Coffee more than six weeks past its roast date loses its sweetness and aromatics, which leaves the bitterness more exposed. Buy smaller bags more often.

## 7. The puck is uneven

Clumps and uneven tamping cause channeling. Water rushes through weak spots and over extracts those parts of the puck while under extracting the rest. The result can taste bitter and sour at the same time.

## The one that is not your fault: your taste buds

People differ in how strongly they taste bitterness. Some people carry genes that make them much more sensitive to certain bitter compounds. If your friends enjoy a shot you find harsh, you may simply be a more sensitive taster. In that case, choose lighter roasts, shorter ratios, or milk drinks, and do not feel bad about it.

## Where to start

Start with the first two. In our experience, grind size and shot length account for most bitter shots at home. Once those are in range, work through temperature, cleaning and beans.

documents.title: Bitter espresso from a new grinder: a small test
documents.text:
When I replaced my old blade grinder with a flat burr grinder, my shots suddenly tasted much more bitter, even though I kept the same beans, dose and ratio. I wanted to understand why, so I ran a small test over a weekend.

## The setup

- Same bag of medium roast beans, 12 days after roasting
- Dose of 18 grams, yield of 36 grams
- Water at 93 °C
- Grinder settings changed in single steps from fine to coarse
- Each shot measured with a cheap refractometer for total dissolved solids (TDS), then converted to extraction yield

## Results

| Grind step | Shot time | TDS | Extraction yield | Taste note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 (finest tested) | 41 s | 11.2% | 22.4% | Bitter, dry finish |
| 6 | 34 s | 10.6% | 21.2% | Slightly bitter |
| 8 | 29 s | 10.1% | 20.2% | Balanced, sweet |
| 10 | 24 s | 9.4% | 18.8% | Bright, a little thin |
| 12 (coarsest tested) | 19 s | 8.6% | 17.2% | Sour |

## What happened

The new grinder produces far fewer fine particles than the old one, so the same setting number does not mean the same grind. My old habit was to grind at setting 4 because that gave a good flow on the old grinder. On the new one, setting 4 over extracted the coffee to more than 22 percent, which is where bitterness starts for most people.

Once I moved to setting 8, the shot ran in 29 seconds, extraction dropped to about 20 percent, and the bitterness went away.

## Lessons

1. A new grinder needs a fresh dial-in. Do not trust old numbers.
2. Better grinders can extract more, because the water flows more evenly. That is good, but it means you may need a coarser setting.
3. Shot time was a decent guide on its own. Every shot over 33 seconds tasted bitter in my test.

## Limits of this test

This was one coffee, one machine and one taster, with a refractometer that is not lab grade. I would not treat these numbers as general rules. The pattern, though, matches what most guides describe: finer grinds and longer shots push extraction up, and bitterness follows.

documents.title: A glossary of espresso taste words
documents.text:
Baristas use a handful of words to describe what goes wrong with a shot. Knowing them makes it easier to read recipes, follow advice and describe your own coffee.

**Acidity.** A bright, lively quality, often fruity. Pleasant acidity is a good thing. Too much, with no sweetness to balance it, reads as sour.

**Astringency.** A drying, puckering sensation, felt more than tasted. It often comes from channeling or from very fine particles that over extract. People often call it bitterness.

**Body.** How heavy the coffee feels in the mouth. Ristretto shots have more body; long shots have less.

**Bitterness.** A heavy, lingering taste at the back of the tongue. A little is part of espresso. Too much usually means over extraction, a dark roast, or a dirty machine.

**Channeling.** When water finds a path of least resistance through the puck. Part of the coffee over extracts and part under extracts, so the shot can taste bitter and sour at once.

**Crema.** The foam on top of a fresh shot, made of oils and gas from fresh coffee. Crema itself tastes bitter, which is why some people stir it in or skim it off.

**Extraction yield.** The percentage of the coffee's dry mass that dissolves into the drink. Many people find 18 to 22 percent tastes balanced. Higher values tend to taste bitter.

**Finish.** The taste that stays after you swallow. A clean, sweet finish is a good sign. A dry, harsh finish is a sign of over extraction.

**Over extraction.** Dissolving too much from the coffee, including the slow, bitter compounds. Caused by fine grinds, long shots, high temperatures, or uneven extraction.

**Ratio.** The weight of coffee out divided by the weight of coffee in. A 1:2 ratio means 36 grams of espresso from 18 grams of grounds.

**Ristretto.** A short shot, often around 1:1 to 1:1.5. Usually sweeter and less bitter than a normal shot, with more body.

**Sweetness.** The quality that makes a shot pleasant to drink straight. It comes from the middle of extraction, after the acids and before the bitter compounds.

**Under extraction.** Dissolving too little. Usually tastes sour, salty and thin. Caused by coarse grinds, short shots, or water that is too cool.

Using these words precisely helps. "Bitter and dry" points to over extraction and channeling; "bitter and smoky" points to the roast. The fix depends on which one you mean.

queries.query: How do I fix bitter espresso?

documents.title: How to fix bitter espresso in six steps
documents.text:
Fix bitter espresso by working through one variable at a time, starting with the ones that change the taste most. Here is the order that works for most home setups.

1. **Grind coarser.** If your shot takes longer than about 30 seconds, move the grinder one or two steps coarser. Grind is the single biggest lever on extraction.
2. **Shorten the ratio.** Weigh the coffee in and the espresso out. If you are pulling more than twice the dose, try stopping at exactly 1:2, for example 18 grams in and 36 grams out.
3. **Lower the temperature.** If your machine allows it, drop the brew temperature by 1 to 2 °C. This helps most with medium and dark roasts.
4. **Fix your puck prep.** Break up clumps, level the grounds and tamp flat. Uneven pucks cause channeling, which tastes bitter and sour at once.
5. **Clean the machine.** Scrub the basket and shower screen, and backflush if your machine supports it. Rancid oils add a stale bitterness to every shot.
6. **Change the beans.** If you still find every shot bitter, try a lighter roast with a recent roast date.

## How much does each step help?

We pulled 48 test shots with the same medium roast and asked three tasters to score bitterness from 1 to 10. Starting from a slow 40 second shot, the changes stacked up like this:

| Change | Average bitterness score |
| --- | --- |
| Starting shot (40 s, 1:2.5) | 7.8 |
| Grind two steps coarser (29 s) | 5.1 |
| Ratio cut to 1:2 | 4.4 |
| Temperature down 2 °C | 3.9 |
| Better puck prep | 3.6 |

The first change did most of the work. The rest were smaller, but together they took a shot most tasters would not finish to one they liked.

## A note on patience

Pull at least two shots after each change before you judge it. The first shot after a grind change can still contain grounds from the old setting.

## Which fix to try first

If you only have time for one change, choose based on the shot time:

- **Slow shot (over 32 seconds):** go coarser. This fixes the problem in most cases.
- **Normal shot (25 to 32 seconds):** shorten the ratio or lower the temperature.
- **Fast shot (under 25 seconds) that is still bitter:** check for channeling and stale or very dark beans.

## Common mistakes

The most common mistake is changing several things at once. If you grind coarser, lower the temperature and switch beans in a single session, you will not know which change helped, and you will have to start again with the next bag.

The second most common mistake is judging by the first shot after a grind change. Grinders hold a small amount of coffee from the previous setting, so purge a few grams before pulling the shot you plan to taste. The third is ignoring the cup: a cold cup pulls heat out of the espresso and makes it taste harsher than it is.

documents.title: Bitter espresso? Try these tips
documents.text:
If your espresso tastes bitter, do not worry, it happens to everyone. Here are some tips that might help you get a better cup at home.

First, try changing your grind. Sometimes a coarser grind helps. You might need to experiment a bit to find the right setting for your beans and your machine.

Second, think about your beans. Fresh beans are always better. Look for beans from a local roaster if you can. Dark roasts can be bitter, so you might want to try something lighter.

Third, keep your machine clean. A dirty machine can make your coffee taste bad. Clean it often and follow the instructions that came with it.

Fourth, try a different recipe. Some people like their espresso short and strong, and some people like it longer. Play with the amount of coffee and water until it tastes right to you.

Fifth, check your water. Filtered water can make your coffee taste better than tap water, especially if your tap water tastes of chlorine.

Finally, remember that making good espresso takes practice. Do not give up if your first few shots are not perfect. Every barista started somewhere. The more you practice, the better your coffee will be, and soon you will be making espresso as good as your favorite cafe.

We hope these tips help you enjoy your coffee more. If you have any other tips, share them in the comments below. And if you want to learn more about coffee, check out our other articles on brewing methods and bean origins.

documents.title: Dialing in espresso: a practical method
documents.text:
Dialing in means adjusting your recipe until a coffee tastes the way you want. When the problem is bitterness, a structured method saves beans and frustration.

Start with a fixed recipe and change only the grind at first. A good starting recipe for a double shot is 18 grams of coffee, 36 grams of liquid, and a target time of 25 to 30 seconds. Pull a shot and taste it.

If the shot is bitter and slow, grind coarser. If it is bitter and fast, the grind is not the problem, so leave it and look elsewhere. If it is sour and fast, grind finer. Keep adjusting the grind in small steps until the time lands in the target window and the taste is close.

Once the time is right, use the ratio to fine-tune. If the shot is still a little bitter, stop it earlier, at 1:1.8 or 1:1.7. If it tastes strong but hollow, let it run a little longer.

Temperature is the third dial. Many home machines let you set it in steps of one degree. For a bitter medium or dark roast, try going down one or two degrees. For a bitter light roast, which is less common, check your grind and puck prep first, because light roasts usually need heat.

Keep notes. A simple log of dose, yield, time, temperature, and a one-word taste note will tell you more in a week than guessing will in a month. Most people find that a coffee is dialed in after five to eight shots, and that a new bag of the same coffee needs only one or two small adjustments.

A final tip: taste with a spoon. Stir the shot, then taste a spoonful. The top layer of crema is more bitter than the rest of the shot and can mislead you.

Once you have a recipe you like, write it on the bag or in a notebook. When you open the next bag of the same coffee, start from that recipe instead of from scratch. Beans from the same roaster and farm behave similarly from bag to bag, so you will usually need only a small grind change.

If you switch between coffees often, note the roast level next to each recipe. Over a few months you will build a personal table of starting points, and dialing in a new coffee will take two or three shots instead of eight.

documents.title: Fixing bitterness without buying anything
documents.text:
You do not need a new grinder or machine to make less bitter espresso. Most of the fixes are free and depend on technique.

The cheapest fix is a scale. Weighing your shot output stops you from running shots too long, which is the most common cause of bitterness at home. If you do not own a scale, a kitchen scale that reads in single grams is fine.

Next, adjust the grind on the grinder you already have. Even basic burr grinders have enough steps to move a shot from slow to normal. Change it slightly, pull two shots, and taste.

Clean what you have. Remove the shower screen if you can and scrub it. Soak the portafilter basket in hot water with a little coffee machine cleaner or plain baking soda. Run plain water through the group head after every session. Many people notice a big drop in bitterness after the first deep clean.

Temperature surfing helps on machines without temperature control. On a single boiler machine, run water through the group head for a few seconds just before you pull a shot. That flushes out overheated water and brings the temperature down.

Finally, change how you drink it. If you have a dark roast you cannot finish, use it for milk drinks, where the bitterness is softened, and buy a medium roast for straight espresso next time.

Pre-ground coffee deserves a special mention. Coffee ground for espresso goes stale within hours, not weeks, because grinding exposes a huge amount of surface to the air. If you are using a bag of pre-ground coffee, most of the fixes above will only help a little. Buying whole beans and grinding just before each shot is the single best upgrade you can make, and a basic hand grinder costs much less than a new machine.

documents.title: Bitter shots: grind, ratio, or temperature?
documents.text:
Many guides list a dozen fixes for bitter espresso. In practice three variables do almost all of the work, and it helps to know how they compare.

| Variable | How it reduces bitterness | Typical change | Effect size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grind size | Less surface area, faster flow | One or two steps coarser | Large |
| Ratio | Stops before the bitter tail | From 1:2.5 to 1:2 | Medium |
| Temperature | Slows extraction of slow compounds | Down 1 to 3 °C | Small to medium |

Grind is first because it changes both the speed of the shot and the amount of surface the water can reach. A one step change on a typical grinder can move shot time by 4 to 6 seconds.

Ratio is second. The last third of a long shot contains a lot of bitterness and little sweetness, so trimming it is effective. It is also the easiest change to make precisely if you use a scale.

Temperature is third. It has a real effect, but a smaller one, and many machines cannot change it at all. It matters most for dark roasts, where a few degrees can separate pleasant from harsh.

Two other variables are worth a mention. Dose changes resistance and strength together, so it is harder to reason about; keep it fixed while you adjust the others. Pre-infusion can reduce channeling, which reduces the mixed sour and bitter taste, but it also lengthens contact time.

Use the table as a checklist: change the grind until the time is right, use the ratio to fine-tune, and reach for temperature last.

documents.title: Notes from a cafe training session on bitter espresso
documents.text:
New staff at a cafe tend to make the same mistakes with bitter shots, so training usually covers the fixes in a set order. These are notes from one such session, cleaned up for home use.

The trainer started with tasting. Everyone pulled one shot that ran very long and one that ran very short, then tasted them side by side. The long shot was bitter and dry. The short shot was sour and salty. Tasting both made it much easier to name what was wrong with later shots.

Then came the routine for fixing a bitter shot. First, check the time. A double shot that runs past 32 or 33 seconds is usually too slow, so the grinder goes one notch coarser. Second, check the yield on the scale. Shots in the cafe were stopped at 2 times the dose, never by eye. Third, check the puck. A puck with a hole in it or a wet, soupy surface points to channeling or to a dose that is too small for the basket.

The trainer also covered the machine. Group heads are flushed between every shot, baskets are wiped dry, and the machine is backflushed with detergent at the end of each day. In a busy cafe a skipped cleaning shows up in the taste by the next afternoon.

The last part of the session was about beans. The cafe's espresso blend is roasted to a medium level and rested for about a week before use. Beans used too fresh were hard to dial in, and beans more than about a month old tasted flat and bitter no matter what anyone did.

The main lesson was to change one thing at a time and taste after every change.

documents.title: A decision tree for fixing a bitter shot
documents.text:
When a shot tastes bitter, the fastest way to fix it is to ask a few questions in order. Each answer points to one change. Make that change, pull another shot, and start again from the top.

## Step 1: How long did the shot take?

- **More than 35 seconds:** the grind is probably too fine. Go one or two steps coarser and stop here for now.
- **Between 25 and 35 seconds:** go to step 2.
- **Less than 25 seconds:** a fast shot that tastes bitter is unusual. Go to step 4.

## Step 2: What was the ratio?

Weigh the espresso in the cup and divide by the dose.

- **More than 1:2.5:** the shot ran too long. Stop it earlier, at about 1:2.
- **Between 1:1.5 and 1:2.5:** go to step 3.

## Step 3: What is the water temperature?

- **Above 94 °C:** lower it by two degrees.
- **93 °C or below:** go to step 4.

## Step 4: How dark is the roast?

- **Dark or very dark (oily beans, smoky smell):** the bitterness is mostly from the roast. Use a shorter ratio, such as 1:1.5, and a lower temperature, around 90 °C. Or try a medium roast.
- **Medium or light:** go to step 5.

## Step 5: When did you last clean the machine?

- **More than a week ago, or never:** backflush the group head, scrub the shower screen and soak the basket and portafilter. Then pull a fresh shot.
- **Recently:** go to step 6.

## Step 6: What does the spent puck look like?

- **Holes, cracks or a wet, soupy surface:** channeling. Break up clumps before tamping, tamp level, and make sure the dose fits the basket.
- **Firm and even:** go back to step 1 and make a smaller grind change. Bitterness can come from being just a little too fine.

## Why one change at a time

If you change grind and temperature together and the shot improves, you will not know which one helped. Worse, one change might help and the other might hurt, so the net result looks like nothing happened. One change per shot is slower in the moment but faster overall.

Most people get through this tree in three to five shots.

documents.title: Fixing bitter espresso: what each change does
documents.text:
Advice on bitter espresso is everywhere, but it rarely says how big each effect is. We pulled 120 shots with one medium roast coffee on two home machines and changed one variable at a time from a bitter starting point (18 grams in, 45 grams out, 38 seconds, 95 °C). A panel of four tasters scored bitterness from 1 (none) to 10 (very bitter).

## Results

| Change from the bitter baseline | Average bitterness score | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline (no change) | 7.8 | |
| Grind two steps coarser | 5.1 | -2.7 |
| Stop at 36 g instead of 45 g | 5.6 | -2.2 |
| Water at 92 °C instead of 95 °C | 6.9 | -0.9 |
| Fresh beans (8 days) instead of old (7 weeks) | 6.7 | -1.1 |
| Clean group head and basket | 7.0 | -0.8 |
| Grind coarser and stop at 36 g together | 3.4 | -4.4 |

## What this suggests

Grind size and shot length had by far the largest effects. Each one alone cut bitterness by more than two points. Together they cut it by more than four, bringing the shot close to what our tasters called balanced.

Temperature, bean freshness and cleaning each helped by about one point. They are worth doing, but they will not rescue a shot that is badly over extracted.

## Caveats

These results come from one coffee and four tasters, so the exact numbers will not transfer to your kitchen. Darker roasts would likely respond more to temperature, and a machine that had never been cleaned would likely benefit more from cleaning. The order of the effects, though, matches what experienced baristas tell beginners: fix grind and ratio first, then fine tune.

## A practical order

1. Adjust the grind until the shot runs 25 to 32 seconds.
2. Stop at a 1:2 ratio.
3. Taste. If it is still bitter, lower the temperature by one or two degrees.
4. If it is still bitter, check bean freshness and clean the machine.

Following this order, most of our test shots reached a bitterness score below 4 within four attempts.

documents.title: Ask a barista: quick answers about bitter shots
documents.text:
We collected the questions customers ask most often at the bar about bitter espresso at home, with short answers from our training team.

**My shots are bitter. What is the very first thing to try?**
Grind coarser. It is the single change most likely to help, and it costs nothing.

**How do I know if I ground too fine?**
The shot runs slowly, often past 35 seconds, and the stream turns thin and pale early. The taste is heavy and the finish is dry.

**Should I tamp lighter?**
Usually not. Tamp pressure matters much less than people think once the coffee is compressed. Keep your tamp consistent and change the grind.

**Is a shorter shot less bitter?**
Generally yes. The bitter compounds come out last, so stopping earlier, at about twice the dose in weight, leaves more of them behind.

**Can I fix bitterness with the temperature setting?**
Sometimes. Dropping one or two degrees helps with dark roasts. With lighter roasts it may make the shot sour instead.

**Do I need new beans?**
If your bag is more than six weeks past roasting, fresh beans will taste sweeter. Dark, oily beans will always be somewhat bitter.

**How often should I clean the machine?**
Rinse the group head after every session, backflush with water weekly if your machine allows it, and use a cleaning powder about once a month. Soak the basket and portafilter at the same time.

**Why is my latte bitter but my espresso fine?**
Check the milk. Overheated milk loses its sweetness. Aim for a jug that is hot to touch but not too hot to hold for a couple of seconds.

**Does the cup matter?**
A cold cup cools the shot fast, and cooler espresso tastes more bitter and less sweet. Warm the cup on the machine or with hot water.

**What if nothing works?**
Pull one shot very fast and one very slow, and taste both. If both are bitter, the beans or the machine are the problem, not your recipe.

documents.title: I fixed my bitter espresso by changing the water
documents.text:
For three months, I chased bitterness in my espresso. I changed grinders, tried five different coffees, and adjusted my recipe over and over. My shots ran in 28 seconds at a 1:2 ratio, which every guide said was right, and they still had a harsh, chalky bitterness at the end. The fix turned out to be the water.

## How I figured it out

A friend brought over a bottle of water she used for her own coffee and suggested we pull two shots side by side: one with my tap water and one with hers. Same beans, same grind, same recipe. The difference was obvious. Her shot was rounder and sweeter. Mine had the same harsh edge it always had.

My tap water turned out to be very hard. The local water report listed a hardness of about 300 milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate. Many coffee guides suggest something closer to 50 to 150.

## Why water matters

Water is more than 90 percent of a shot of espresso. The minerals in it change how coffee compounds dissolve. Very hard water can mute sweetness and acidity and leave a dull, chalky bitterness. Very soft water can make coffee taste flat and sour. Hard water also builds up scale inside the machine, which can affect temperature over time.

## What I changed

I started using filtered water from a jug filter, and later mixed my own water from distilled water and a small packet of minerals sold for coffee. Both helped. The mixed water was the best, but the jug filter got me most of the way.

## Results after a month

- Bitterness at the end of the shot is mostly gone.
- I could go back to a slightly finer grind than before without the shot turning harsh.
- The descaling light on my machine has not come on since.

## Would this work for you?

Only if your water is the problem. If your shots run slow or long, fix the grind and ratio first. But if your recipe is in range and the bitterness will not go away, try one shot with bottled or filtered water. It takes five minutes and might save you months.

documents.title: Bitter espresso fix: everything you need to know
documents.text:
Bitter espresso is a common problem. Many people want to know how to fix bitter espresso. In this article we will tell you everything you need to know about fixing bitter espresso.

First, it is important to understand that espresso can be bitter for many reasons. Fixing bitter espresso means finding the reason and then fixing it. This can take some time, but it is worth it, because good espresso is delicious.

One way to fix bitter espresso is to use better coffee beans. Better coffee beans make better espresso. You can find good coffee beans at many stores and online. Look for coffee beans that you like.

Another way to fix bitter espresso is to make sure your equipment is good. Good equipment makes it easier to make good espresso. Many people say that the grinder is important. Some people say that the machine is important. Both are important.

You can also fix bitter espresso by practicing. The more you practice making espresso, the better you will get. Watching videos and reading guides can also help you learn how to fix bitter espresso.

Some people add sugar to bitter espresso. Sugar can make bitter espresso taste less bitter. Milk can also help. If you add milk, you can make a latte or a cappuccino. These drinks are less bitter than espresso.

It is also a good idea to ask for help. Baristas at your local coffee shop may be able to give you tips on how to fix bitter espresso. Friends who make espresso at home may also have tips.

Finally, remember to be patient. Fixing bitter espresso can take time. Do not give up! With some effort, you can fix bitter espresso and enjoy great espresso at home.

We hope this guide to fixing bitter espresso was helpful. Fixing bitter espresso is easier than you think when you know what to do. Good luck, and enjoy your espresso!

Summary: To fix bitter espresso, try better beans, check your equipment, practice, add milk or sugar if you like, ask for help, and be patient. These are the most important tips for fixing bitter espresso.

documents.title: A cleaning routine that keeps stale bitterness out of your espresso
documents.text:
Some bitterness has nothing to do with your recipe. Coffee oils stick to every metal surface they touch, and within a day or two they go rancid. If you have dialed in carefully and your shots still taste stale and bitter, a cleaning routine may be what is missing.

## What to clean, and how often

| Part | Daily | Weekly | Monthly |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Group head and gasket | Wipe and flush with water | Backflush with water (if supported) | Backflush with cleaning powder |
| Shower screen | Rinse | Brush | Remove and soak |
| Basket and portafilter | Rinse and wipe | Soak in hot water | Soak in cleaning solution |
| Steam wand | Purge and wipe after each use | Soak the tip | Check the holes for blockage |
| Grinder | Brush out loose grounds | Run cleaning pellets or rice-free cleaner | Remove burrs and brush |
| Water tank | Refill with fresh water | Rinse | Descale as the manual says |

## Signs that cleaning is overdue

- Shots taste stale, sharp or "dirty" even with fresh beans.
- The water from the group head (with no coffee) smells like old coffee.
- The shower screen has a dark film or visible grounds stuck to it.
- The first shot of the day tastes much worse than the third.

## A quick test

Run hot water through the group head into a clean white cup, without coffee. Look at the color and smell it. If it is brown or smells of coffee, oils are building up. After a backflush with cleaning powder, the water should be clear and smell of nothing.

## Do not forget the grinder

Old coffee left in the grinder goes stale and gets mixed into the next dose. Some grinders hold several grams. If you only make one or two shots a day, purge a small amount before your first shot, and brush out the chute regularly.

## How much difference does it make?

In a café we trained, the team skipped their weekly backflush for three weeks during a busy period. Customer comments about "burnt" or "bitter" coffee went from about two a week to nine a week. After a deep clean, the comments fell back to two within a week. Clean equipment will not fix a bad recipe, but dirty equipment can ruin a good one.

queries.query: What water temperature should I use for espresso?

documents.title: Espresso water temperature by roast level
documents.text:
Use water between 90 and 96 °C for espresso, and match the temperature to the roast: hotter for light roasts, cooler for dark roasts. Most machines ship set to about 93 °C, which is a reasonable middle.

## Recommended starting points

| Roast level | Starting temperature | Range to explore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Light | 95 °C | 94 to 96 °C |
| Medium | 93 °C | 92 to 94 °C |
| Medium dark | 92 °C | 91 to 93 °C |
| Dark | 90 °C | 89 to 91 °C |

## Why roast level matters

Light roasts are dense and less soluble, so they need more energy to extract fully. At low temperatures they taste sour and thin. Dark roasts are more porous and already contain a lot of bitter roasting compounds, so hot water pulls out bitterness quickly. Lowering the temperature gives you a sweeter, rounder cup.

## How big is the effect?

In side by side tests, a 2 °C change is usually easy to taste in a dark roast and subtle in a light one. Going from 96 to 90 °C with the same grind and ratio typically lowers the extraction yield by about 1 percentage point, which is enough to move a shot from harsh to balanced.

## Measuring temperature

The number on the display is not always the temperature at the coffee. On many machines the water cools by 1 to 4 °C between the boiler and the puck. If you want to know your real brew temperature, a thermocouple placed in the basket gives the most accurate reading. Otherwise, treat the display as a dial, change it in small steps, and trust your taste.

## Machines without a temperature setting

Single boiler machines without a PID controller swing several degrees during a session. Flush a little water before each shot to get a more consistent starting point.

## Temperature and the rest of the recipe

Temperature is the third dial to reach for, after grind and ratio. Raising it has a similar effect to grinding a little finer: more extraction, more body and, past a point, more bitterness. Lowering it is similar to grinding a little coarser. If you have just changed your grind, wait a few shots before you touch the temperature, so you can tell the two effects apart.

## A simple routine

1. Set the machine to the starting point for your roast in the table above.
2. Dial in the grind until the shot runs 25 to 30 seconds at a 1:2 ratio.
3. Taste. If it is bitter, lower the temperature by 1 °C. If it is sour, raise it by 1 °C.
4. Repeat step 3 until the shot is balanced, then write the setting down.

Most coffees settle within 2 °C of the starting point.

documents.title: What temperature is best for espresso?
documents.text:
The best temperature for espresso is a question that comes up a lot. Some people say hotter is better and some people say cooler is better. The truth is that it depends on many things.

Water that is too cold will not extract enough flavor from the coffee. Your espresso will taste weak and sour. Water that is too hot can burn the coffee and make it bitter. You want something in between.

Most experts agree that the right temperature is somewhere a little below boiling. Boiling water is too hot for espresso. Most espresso machines are set at the factory to a good temperature, so for most people the default setting is fine.

If your machine lets you change the temperature, you can experiment. Try making it a little hotter or a little cooler and see what you like. Everyone has different taste, so there is no perfect answer for everyone.

Some machines take a long time to heat up. Make sure you let your machine warm up fully before making coffee. If you make coffee too soon, the water may not be hot enough, and the cups and portafilter will still be cold, which also cools the shot.

Also remember that the temperature of the cup matters. A cold cup will cool your espresso quickly. Warm your cup with hot water before you pull your shot, and drink your espresso soon after it is made for the best flavor.

In summary, do not worry too much about temperature. Use the default setting and focus on fresh beans and a good grind. Those will make a bigger difference to your coffee than a few degrees.

documents.title: Brew temperature and extraction: a closer look
documents.text:
Temperature changes how quickly coffee dissolves, but it does not change every compound equally. That is why a few degrees can shift the flavor of a shot, not just its strength.

At higher temperatures, water dissolves the slow, heavy compounds more readily. In practice that means more body and more bitterness. At lower temperatures, the fast dissolving acids make up a larger share of the cup, so the shot tastes brighter and sometimes sour.

Here is how temperature interacts with the other variables:

- **Grind.** A finer grind and a higher temperature both raise extraction. If you raise one, you may need to lower the other.
- **Ratio.** A longer ratio at a high temperature is the classic recipe for a bitter shot. If you like long shots, keep the temperature moderate.
- **Roast.** Light roasts tolerate and often need 94 to 96 °C. Dark roasts often taste best at 89 to 91 °C.
- **Pre-infusion.** A gentle pre-infusion at a lower pressure can make a high temperature more forgiving by reducing channeling.

Machines also differ in how stable they are. Dual boiler and PID controlled machines hold their temperature within about half a degree from shot to shot. Simpler single boiler machines can swing by 5 °C or more depending on when the heater last switched on. On those machines, consistency matters more than the exact setting. Flushing the group the same way before each shot gives you a repeatable starting point.

If you only remember one thing, remember this: when a shot tastes bitter and the grind and ratio are already right, lower the temperature by one or two degrees and taste again.

documents.title: Temperature surfing on a single boiler machine
documents.text:
Many entry level espresso machines have one boiler and a simple thermostat. They do not let you set a temperature, and they run hotter or cooler depending on when the heating element last turned on. Temperature surfing is the habit of timing your shot to land at a consistent point in that cycle.

The basic routine is simple. Let the machine heat up fully, which takes 15 to 20 minutes on most small machines, including the group head. Watch the heating light. When it turns off, the boiler has just reached its upper limit and is at its hottest. Run water through the group head for a few seconds, then lock in the portafilter and pull your shot.

How long you flush depends on the machine and on the roast. For dark roasts, a longer flush of four to six seconds brings the temperature down and reduces bitterness. For light roasts, a short flush or none at all keeps the water hotter.

The trick only works if you repeat it the same way each time. Count the seconds of the flush and start the shot at the same point after the light changes. Within a few days the routine becomes automatic, and your shots become much more consistent.

Some owners go further and fit an aftermarket temperature controller. That is a bigger project, and for most people careful surfing is enough to tame bitter shots.

A few practical cautions. Do not flush so long that the boiler refills and starts heating again, or you will end up hotter than before. Use a cup or a jug under the group head so you can see the water: on many machines the first water sputters and steams, which tells you it was above brewing temperature, and when the stream calms down the temperature is closer to where you want it.

documents.title: Espresso temperature myths
documents.text:
A lot of advice about espresso temperature is repeated without much thought. Here are four common claims and what actually holds up.

**Myth 1: Hotter is always better.** Higher temperatures do extract more, but more is not always better. With dark roasts, the extra extraction is mostly bitterness. Many cafes run their dark blends at 90 or 91 °C for exactly this reason.

**Myth 2: The display shows the brew temperature.** It usually shows the boiler temperature. The water can lose a few degrees on its way through the group head and into the puck. Two machines set to 93 °C can brew at noticeably different temperatures.

**Myth 3: Temperature matters more than grind.** For most shots, grind has the bigger effect. A one step grind change usually moves the taste more than a one degree temperature change. Fix the grind first, then use temperature to fine-tune.

**Myth 4: You need an expensive machine to control temperature.** A precise controller helps, but a consistent flushing routine on a basic machine gets you most of the way there. Consistency is the real goal, because you cannot dial in a recipe when the temperature changes from shot to shot.

**What holds up.** Light roasts usually want more heat and dark roasts less. Small changes, one or two degrees at a time, are easier to judge than big jumps. Taste is the final test, since beans from different farms and roasters respond differently.

If you are unsure where to start, set the machine to 93 °C, dial in the grind and ratio, and then move the temperature up or down one degree at a time while tasting.

documents.title: Temperature, pressure and time: the three dials of espresso
documents.text:
Every espresso machine controls three things: how hot the water is, how hard it is pushed, and how long it runs. Understanding how they fit together makes it easier to choose a temperature.

Pressure is usually fixed at around 9 bar on home machines. Time is mostly controlled by grind size and dose. Temperature is the dial that many people never touch, but it shapes flavor in a way the other two cannot.

A typical starting recipe looks like this:

| Dial | Common setting | What it mainly affects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature | 93 °C | Balance of acids and bitterness |
| Pressure | 9 bar | Flow rate and crema |
| Time | 25 to 30 seconds | Overall extraction |
| Ratio | 1:2 | Strength and body |

When you change temperature, keep the others fixed. A shot that ran 28 seconds at 93 °C will run at almost the same speed at 91 °C, but it will taste a little softer and less bitter. That makes temperature a clean way to adjust flavor without redoing your whole recipe.

The usual range for espresso is 88 to 96 °C. Below that range most coffees taste sour. Above it, most coffees taste harsh. Within it, the right setting depends on the roast and on your taste.

## Why not use boiling water?

Water at 100 °C extracts too aggressively for espresso. Because espresso uses fine grounds and high pressure, it is already an efficient way to extract coffee, and boiling water on top of that pulls out bitterness very quickly. Brewing below boiling, usually 7 to 10 degrees below, keeps the shot balanced.

## Changing temperature in practice

Change the temperature in steps of one degree and pull at least two shots at each setting before you judge it. If your machine reports temperature in Fahrenheit, one step of 2 °F is close to one step of 1 °C. Keep the grind, dose and ratio the same while you test, so that temperature is the only thing that changes.

documents.title: Espresso brew temperature chart by roast and process
documents.text:
The best brew temperature depends mostly on how dark the coffee is roasted, and a little on how it was processed. The chart below gives starting points. Treat them as a place to begin, then adjust by taste.

## Starting temperatures

| Roast level | Washed coffee | Natural or honey processed | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Light | 94 to 96 °C | 93 to 95 °C | Light roasts are dense and resist extraction; hotter water helps |
| Medium light | 93 to 95 °C | 92 to 94 °C | A good place for most single origin espresso |
| Medium | 92 to 94 °C | 91 to 93 °C | Most espresso blends sit here |
| Medium dark | 90 to 92 °C | 90 to 92 °C | Lower temperature softens roast bitterness |
| Dark | 88 to 91 °C | 88 to 91 °C | Go low to keep smoky, ashy flavors down |

## Why roast matters

Lighter roasts are denser and less soluble. Hotter water helps dissolve their sugars and acids so they do not taste sour. Darker roasts are more porous and dissolve easily, and they already carry bitter compounds from the roasting. Cooler water extracts less of those compounds.

## Why processing matters, a little

Natural and honey processed coffees often taste fruitier and sweeter, and some baristas find they turn harsh at the top of the temperature range. A degree lower is a reasonable starting point. The effect is smaller than the effect of roast level.

## How to adjust

Change the temperature in steps of one or two degrees and keep everything else the same. Taste for these signs:

- **Sour, thin, sharp:** raise the temperature.
- **Bitter, harsh, dry:** lower the temperature.
- **Flat, dull:** try a degree higher; flatness often means not enough extraction.

## What the display means

The temperature on a machine's display is usually the boiler temperature, not the temperature of the water hitting the coffee. The water at the puck is often one to four degrees cooler, depending on the machine. Two machines set to 93 °C can therefore brew quite differently. If your machine has an offset setting in its manual, use it. Otherwise, rely on taste.

documents.title: Does a two-degree change really matter? A blind tasting
documents.text:
Guides often tell you to change brew temperature by a degree or two. We wanted to know whether people can actually taste that difference, so we ran a blind tasting with eight regular espresso drinkers.

## Method

- One medium roast blend, 10 days after roasting
- 18 grams in, 36 grams out, ground to run about 28 seconds at 93 °C
- Shots pulled at 90, 93 and 96 °C on a machine with a calibrated thermometer at the group
- Grind unchanged across temperatures, so shot times shifted slightly
- Each taster received three cups in random order, labeled only with letters, and ranked them for bitterness and for overall preference
- Repeated over two days, for 16 rankings in total

## Results

| Temperature | Ranked most bitter | Ranked least bitter | Ranked favorite |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 90 °C | 1 of 16 | 11 of 16 | 6 of 16 |
| 93 °C | 3 of 16 | 4 of 16 | 8 of 16 |
| 96 °C | 12 of 16 | 1 of 16 | 2 of 16 |

The 96 °C shots were ranked most bitter in 12 of 16 rankings. Between 90 and 93 °C the bitterness ranking was clear, but preference was split: some tasters liked the extra body and sweetness at 93 °C, while others preferred the softer 90 °C shot.

## Could tasters tell 90 from 93?

When we asked tasters to pick out the odd one in sets of three (two cups at one temperature, one at the other), they found the odd cup 10 times out of 16. Guessing at random would give about 5 or 6 out of 16. So a three-degree change was noticeable for most people, though not every time.

## What this means for you

A few degrees matters, especially at the hot end, where bitterness rises quickly. A single degree is harder to taste and may be lost in the normal variation between shots. If you are fighting bitterness, a step of two or three degrees down is a fair test. If you are fine tuning a shot you already like, one degree may not be worth worrying about.

## Limits

Eight tasters and one coffee is a small test. A dark roast would likely show stronger differences, and a light roast might favor the hottest setting.

documents.title: Espresso temperature FAQ for new machine owners
documents.text:
New espresso machines come with temperature settings, and many owners are not sure what to do with them. Here are short answers to the questions we hear most.

**What temperature should I start with?**
Around 93 °C is a common default and works for most medium roasts.

**Is hotter always stronger?**
Hotter water extracts more, which can taste stronger, but past a point it mostly adds bitterness. Strength is better controlled with the dose and ratio.

**My machine has no temperature setting. Is that a problem?**
Not necessarily. Many simple machines are set at the factory to a sensible range. You can still adjust extraction with grind and ratio. Some owners use "temperature surfing", running water through the group to cool or heat it before the shot.

**How do I know if my temperature is wrong?**
If shots taste sour even when they run slowly and long, try warmer water. If they taste bitter even when they run quickly, try cooler water.

**Should light and dark roasts use the same temperature?**
No. Light roasts usually do better hotter, around 94 to 96 °C. Dark roasts usually do better cooler, around 88 to 91 °C.

**How long does the machine need to warm up?**
Much longer than the ready light suggests on many machines. The boiler may be hot in a few minutes, but the group head and portafilter take longer. Fifteen to thirty minutes is common for heavier machines. Pulling a blank shot through the portafilter helps it warm up.

**Does a cold portafilter matter?**
Yes. A cold portafilter can pull several degrees out of the water in the first seconds of the shot. Keep the portafilter locked into the group while the machine heats.

**Why does my first shot taste different from the second?**
The first shot often comes from water that has been sitting in the group and lines, which can be cooler or hotter than the set temperature. Run a little water before each shot to stabilize it.

**Does the steam setting affect espresso temperature?**
On single boiler machines, yes. After steaming, the boiler is far too hot for espresso. Let it cool, or run water until the temperature drops, before pulling the next shot.

documents.title: Why the temperature on your display may not be the temperature at the coffee
documents.text:
Most espresso machines show a single brew temperature, but that number is measured somewhere inside the machine, usually in or near the boiler. The water that actually reaches the coffee can be several degrees cooler. Knowing this helps explain why recipes do not always transfer from one machine to another.

## Where the heat goes

Between the boiler and the coffee, water passes through pipes, a valve, the group head and the shower screen. Each part can absorb or release heat. A heavy brass group head that is fully warmed holds the temperature steady. A light group head that has not warmed up can cool the water noticeably.

## Typical offsets

In tests on six home machines with a thermocouple placed in the basket, the difference between the display and the water at the puck ranged widely:

| Machine type | Display setting | Measured at the puck | Offset |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single boiler, small group | 93 °C | 88 °C | -5 °C |
| Single boiler, heavy group | 93 °C | 91 °C | -2 °C |
| Heat exchanger | 93 °C (set by pressure) | 90 to 96 °C | depends on flushing |
| Dual boiler, saturated group | 93 °C | 92.5 °C | -0.5 °C |
| Thermoblock | 93 °C | 89 °C | -4 °C |
| Dual boiler, standard group | 93 °C | 91 °C | -2 °C |

These are examples from a small test, not specifications for any model, but they show how much machines can differ.

## What to do about it

- **Warm everything fully.** Leave the portafilter locked in while the machine heats and run a blank shot before your first real one.
- **Look for an offset setting.** Some machines let you enter an offset so the display shows the temperature at the group.
- **Trust taste over numbers.** If a recipe says 93 °C and the shot tastes sour on your machine, your machine may be brewing cooler. Raise the setting.
- **Be consistent.** The exact number matters less than making every shot the same way, so that you can compare one change at a time.

## A note on heat exchanger machines

Heat exchanger machines heat brew water by passing it through a tube inside the steam boiler. Water that sits in the tube can overheat. Most owners run a short flush before each shot to bring the temperature down to a stable range.

documents.title: Best espresso temperature (updated)
documents.text:
What is the best espresso temperature? This is one of the most common questions about espresso. The best espresso temperature is important for making the best espresso, so it is good to know the best espresso temperature.

Temperature is one of the things that affects espresso. When you make espresso, the water needs to be hot. If the water is not hot enough, the espresso may not taste good. If the water is too hot, the espresso may also not taste good. So the temperature has to be just right.

Most people agree that espresso should be made with hot water, but not boiling water. Boiling water is too hot for espresso. Water that is just below boiling is better. This is the best espresso temperature for most people.

Different coffees may need different temperatures. Some coffees taste better with hotter water. Some coffees taste better with cooler water. You can try different temperatures to find the best espresso temperature for your coffee.

Your machine may have a setting for temperature. If it does, you can change the temperature to see what tastes best. If it does not, you can still make good espresso. Many machines without temperature settings make great espresso.

It is also important to keep your machine clean. A clean machine works better and makes better espresso. Clean your machine often.

The best espresso temperature can depend on your taste. Some people like their espresso one way, and some people like it another way. There is no single right answer for everyone. The best espresso temperature is the one that makes espresso you enjoy.

We will keep updating this page with more information about the best espresso temperature. Bookmark it and come back later!

Key takeaways:
- The best espresso temperature is hot but not boiling.
- Different coffees may need different temperatures.
- Try different temperatures to find what you like.
- Keep your machine clean.
- The best espresso temperature depends on your taste.

documents.title: Altitude, boiling points and espresso
documents.text:
If you live high above sea level, you may have read that water boils at a lower temperature there and wondered whether that changes how you should make espresso. The short answer is that it matters a lot for kettles and pour over, and much less for most espresso machines.

## Why water boils lower at altitude

Air pressure falls as you go up. Lower pressure lets water boil at a lower temperature. At sea level water boils at about 100 °C. At 1,500 meters it boils at about 95 °C, and at 2,500 meters at about 92 °C.

## What that means for kettle brewing

If you make pour over or French press with a kettle, your water simply cannot get as hot at altitude. At 2,500 meters, water straight off the boil is already below the 93 to 96 °C many filter recipes call for. People at high altitude often grind finer or brew longer to make up for the cooler water.

## Why espresso machines are different

Espresso machines heat water inside a sealed boiler or a heating block, under pressure. The pressure inside a closed boiler is not set by the air outside in the same way, so most machines can reach normal brew temperatures at any altitude.

There are two exceptions worth knowing:

1. **Steam boilers and heat exchanger machines** that are controlled by a pressure switch may behave differently at altitude, because the switch reads pressure relative to the outside air. Some owners adjust the pressure setting after moving to a much higher or lower place.
2. **Open systems**, such as stovetop pots, behave more like kettles. The water boils at a lower temperature, and the coffee comes out cooler.

## Practical advice

- With a modern machine with a temperature controller, set the temperature as you would at sea level and adjust by taste.
- With a pressure controlled machine, check the manual for altitude advice and watch the steam pressure gauge.
- With a stovetop pot, expect a slightly sourer cup at high altitude, and try a finer grind.

## Does altitude change the coffee?

Coffee grown at high altitude is often described as denser and brighter, but that is about where the beans were grown, not where you brew them. Roasters usually account for it, and light roasts from high farms may need the hotter end of the temperature range.
