documents.title: Espresso shot time: the 25 to 30 second rule
documents.text:
A standard double espresso should take about 25 to 30 seconds from the moment you start the pump to the moment you stop it, producing roughly twice the weight of the dry coffee. That window is a guide, not a law, but it is where most coffees taste balanced.

## Typical recipes

| Style | Dose | Yield | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ristretto | 18 g | 18 to 27 g | 20 to 25 s |
| Normale | 18 g | 36 g | 25 to 30 s |
| Lungo | 18 g | 54 to 72 g | 30 to 40 s |

## What the time tells you

Shot time is a quick check on your grind. If a normale runs 20 seconds or less, the grind is probably too coarse, and the shot will likely taste sour. If it runs past about 35 seconds, the grind is probably too fine, and the shot will likely taste bitter.

## When to start the timer

People time shots in different ways, which causes a lot of confusion online. Most baristas start the timer when they press the button. Others start it when the first drops appear. The difference can be 5 to 8 seconds, so be consistent and know which method a recipe uses.

## Time is not the goal

Taste always wins. Some light roasts taste best at 32 seconds, and some dark roasts taste best at 24. Use the time window to get close, then adjust by taste. A scale is more useful than a timer: a shot that hits 36 grams in 31 seconds and tastes great is a good shot.

documents.title: How long does espresso take?
documents.text:
How long should espresso take? This is one of the most common questions from new baristas. The answer is that it depends on a lot of things, like your machine, your beans, and how you like your coffee.

Some people say espresso should take about half a minute. Others say it can be shorter or longer. There is no single answer that works for everyone, because every machine is different and every coffee is different.

If your espresso comes out very fast, it might taste weak or sour. If it comes out very slowly, it might taste bitter or burnt. You want it somewhere in the middle. Watch the stream as it comes out. It should look a bit like warm honey.

The color can also tell you something. Good espresso starts dark and gets lighter as the shot goes on. When it starts to look pale and watery, many people stop the shot.

Remember that the time is only one part of making espresso. You also need good beans, the right grind, and a clean machine. Do not focus too much on the clock and forget the other things.

The most important thing is that you enjoy your coffee. If you like your espresso a certain way, that is the right way for you, even if it does not match what the experts say. Try different times and see what tastes best to you. Making espresso is a journey, and you will learn something new with every cup you make.

documents.title: Why shot time varies and what to do about it
documents.text:
You can use the same beans, the same grinder and the same machine and still see shot times jump by several seconds from one day to the next. Here is why, and how to keep your shots consistent.

**Bean age.** Freshly roasted beans release a lot of carbon dioxide, which makes the puck resist water differently. As beans age over the first two or three weeks, shots tend to run faster at the same grind setting. Expect to grind a little finer as a bag gets older.

**Humidity and temperature.** Ground coffee absorbs moisture from the air, and grinders behave differently when they warm up. On humid days, shots often run slower.

**Dose.** Half a gram more or less in the basket changes resistance noticeably. Weigh every dose.

**Distribution and tamping.** Uneven grounds create easy paths for water. A shot that channels may run fast at first and then stall, and the time will mislead you.

**Retention in the grinder.** Many grinders hold a gram or two of old grounds. The first shot of the day can contain stale coffee and run differently from the rest.

What to do about it:

- weigh your dose and your yield every time
- purge a small amount of coffee from the grinder at the start of a session
- adjust the grind in small steps as a bag ages
- use the same distribution and tamping routine for every shot

With those habits, most home baristas can keep shot times within 2 or 3 seconds of their target, which is close enough that taste, not time, becomes the deciding factor.

documents.title: Shot time versus ratio: which matters more?
documents.text:
Ask ten baristas how long an espresso should take and most will say 25 to 30 seconds. Ask what ratio they use and you will hear 1:2 more often than anything else. Both numbers matter, but they do different jobs.

The ratio, the weight of liquid out compared to the weight of coffee in, sets the strength of the shot and decides how far along the extraction curve you stop. The time is mostly a reading of your grind and puck prep. Two shots with the same ratio and very different times taste different, but two shots with the same time and very different ratios taste even more different.

| Shot | Ratio | Time | Typical taste |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1:2 | 28 s | Balanced |
| B | 1:2 | 40 s | Bitter, heavy |
| C | 1:2 | 18 s | Sour, thin |
| D | 1:3 | 28 s | Light, can be bitter |

That is why many modern recipes are written as dose, yield and time together, for example 18 grams in, 36 grams out, in 27 seconds. Use the ratio to decide when to stop, and use the time to check that your grind is in the right place.

If you have to choose, measure weight before time. A scale under the cup prevents the single most common mistake at home, which is running shots far too long.

A practical routine is to put the cup on a scale, start a timer when you press the button, and stop the shot when the scale reaches your target yield. Then look at the time. If it is in the expected window and the shot tastes good, leave everything alone. If the time is off, change the grind, not the yield, and try again.

documents.title: My shot runs in 15 seconds. Help!
documents.text:
A shot that runs in 15 seconds is called a gusher, and it is one of the most common problems with a new grinder or a new bag of beans. The water is finding its way through the coffee too easily, so it does not have time to extract the sugars and body that make espresso taste good. The result is usually sour, salty and thin.

The fix is almost always a finer grind. Move the grinder a few steps finer and pull another shot. Keep going in small steps until the shot runs somewhere between 25 and 30 seconds for a 1:2 ratio.

If you are already at the finest setting and the shot still runs fast, check a few other things. Your dose may be too small for the basket. Most double baskets are designed for 16 to 20 grams. Your beans may be stale, since old coffee resists water less. Or your grinder may not be able to grind fine enough for espresso. Some grinders are built for filter coffee and cannot reach espresso fineness at all.

The opposite problem, a shot that barely drips or takes more than 40 seconds, is a choke. That usually means the grind is too fine or the dose is too large. Go coarser, or take out a gram of coffee.

Both problems are normal when you start. Expect to spend a few shots dialing in every new bag.

One more tip: change the grind only while the grinder is running, if the manual allows it. On many burr grinders, adjusting the setting while the burrs are stopped can jam coffee between them and give you an uneven first dose.

documents.title: Reading the stream: what a good shot looks like
documents.text:
Time is easy to measure, but watching the shot as it pours tells you just as much. Here is what to look for during a typical 25 to 30 second double shot.

In the first 5 to 8 seconds, little or nothing comes out as the puck fills with water. Then the first drops appear, usually dark brown and thick. A good shot then forms a steady, narrow stream that looks like warm syrup. It should not spray, spurt or come out of one side of the basket only. A bottomless portafilter makes this easy to see.

As the shot continues, the color lightens from dark brown to caramel and then toward a pale blond. When most of the stream turns pale, the shot is near its end. Running much longer adds mostly water and the bitter compounds that come out last.

Warning signs:

- a stream that starts within 2 or 3 seconds and runs pale early, which means the grind is too coarse
- a stream that drips for a long time and never forms, which means the grind is too fine
- spurts or jets from the bottom of the basket, which means channeling
- a stream that blonds very early, which often means stale beans

Use what you see together with the scale and the timer. When the stream looks right, the shot reaches its target weight in the expected time, and it tastes balanced, your recipe is dialed in.

A final note on timing: a shot that looks perfect can still taste wrong if the beans are past their best or the machine needs cleaning, so let the stream guide your grind but let taste have the last word.

documents.title: Espresso recipes by the numbers: dose, yield and time
documents.text:
Shot time only makes sense next to dose and yield. The same 30 seconds can produce a short, syrupy ristretto or a long, light shot, depending on the grind and how much comes out. The table below lists common recipes with typical times.

## Common recipes

| Style | Dose in | Yield out | Ratio | Typical time | Taste |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ristretto | 18 g | 18 to 27 g | 1:1 to 1:1.5 | 20 to 30 s | Thick, sweet, intense |
| Traditional espresso | 18 g | 36 g | 1:2 | 25 to 30 s | Balanced, the usual starting point |
| Modern light roast shot | 18 g | 40 to 45 g | 1:2.2 to 1:2.5 | 28 to 35 s | Brighter, clearer, less body |
| Lungo | 18 g | 54 to 72 g | 1:3 to 1:4 | 35 to 45 s | Thin, more bitter, more caffeine per cup |
| Fast "turbo" shot | 18 g | 45 to 55 g | 1:2.5 to 1:3 | 10 to 15 s | Light, clean, coarse grind and lower pressure |
| Single basket | 9 g | 18 g | 1:2 | 22 to 28 s | Similar to a double but harder to keep consistent |

## How to use this table

Pick a style, set the dose and target yield, then adjust the grind until the time falls in the range. If the shot reaches the target yield too fast, grind finer. If it takes too long, grind coarser.

## When the time is out of range

- **Much faster than the range:** the grind is likely too coarse, the dose too small, or the beans stale.
- **Much slower than the range:** the grind is likely too fine, the dose too large, or the puck has clumped.

## Why ranges and not a single number

Beans, roast, grinder and machine all change how fast water moves through the puck. A light roast on a flat burr grinder might taste best at 33 seconds, while a dark blend on a conical grinder might taste best at 24. The ranges above cover most cases, but your taste is the final judge.

## Single baskets

Single baskets are harder to dial in because small differences in dose or distribution have a larger effect. Many cafés use double baskets and split the shot. At home, a double is usually easier to get right.

documents.title: Stop timing from the button: when does a shot start?
documents.text:
Ask ten baristas how long their shots take and you may get ten different ways of measuring. Some start the timer when they press the button, some when the first drop appears, and some when the pump reaches full pressure. The difference can be eight seconds or more, which is why shot times from different sources often do not agree.

## Three common starting points

1. **Button press.** The simplest and most repeatable. Many cafés use it because it is easy to train.
2. **First drop.** Ignores the time the water takes to fill the headspace and soak the puck. Times measured this way are shorter by several seconds.
3. **Full pressure.** Used by some people with machines that have long pre-infusion. It ignores the whole pre-infusion phase.

## How much difference it makes

On a machine with a three second fill and a five second pre-infusion, a shot that takes 30 seconds from the button press takes about 25 seconds from the first drop and about 22 seconds from full pressure. All three numbers describe the same shot.

## Pre-infusion changes the picture

Pre-infusion wets the puck with low pressure before the full pump pressure starts. It can reduce channeling and make shots more even. It also adds time. A recipe written for a machine with no pre-infusion may say 27 seconds, while the same coffee on a machine with ten seconds of pre-infusion may taste best at 35 seconds from the button.

## Which one should you use?

It does not matter much, as long as you:

- use the same method every time,
- note which method a recipe uses before you copy its time,
- judge the shot by taste and yield, not by the clock alone.

For most home baristas, timing from the button press is easiest and is the method most guides assume.

## A better habit

Write down three numbers for every shot: dose, yield and time. Time on its own tells you little. A 30 second shot that yields 25 grams is very different from a 30 second shot that yields 50 grams. When you compare shots, compare all three numbers measured the same way.

## Summary

The common 25 to 30 second guideline usually assumes timing from the button press, a 1:2 ratio, and little or no pre-infusion. If your machine pre-infuses, expect longer times for a shot that tastes just as good.

documents.title: Turbo shots: fast espresso on purpose
documents.text:
Most guides say a shot should take 25 to 30 seconds. A growing number of baristas are deliberately pulling shots in 10 to 15 seconds instead, and some of them taste very good. These are often called turbo shots.

## What a turbo shot is

A turbo shot uses a much coarser grind, a longer ratio (around 1:2.5 to 1:3) and usually lower pump pressure, around 6 bar instead of the usual 9. Water flows through quickly and evenly. Because the grind is coarse, there are fewer fine particles to clog the puck and cause channeling.

## Why it can work

Extraction depends on more than time. A coarse grind with a long ratio and an even flow can reach a similar extraction yield to a traditional shot, just faster. Some people find turbo shots cleaner and sweeter, with less bitterness, especially with light roasts.

## Why it does not always work

- Not every machine can lower its pressure.
- At full 9 bar pressure, a coarse grind may run so fast that the shot tastes sour and thin.
- Dark roasts can taste weak and watery as turbo shots.
- Milk drinks may lose the body people expect.

## A starting recipe

| Setting | Traditional shot | Turbo shot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dose | 18 g | 18 g |
| Yield | 36 g | 50 g |
| Grind | Fine | Much coarser |
| Pressure | 9 bar | About 6 bar |
| Time | 25 to 30 s | 10 to 15 s |

## So is the 25 to 30 second rule wrong?

It is a good rule for traditional espresso on a typical machine. It is not a law of nature. Shot time is the result of grind, dose, pressure and puck preparation, and different combinations can taste good. If your machine can lower its pressure and you like light roasts, try a turbo shot. If not, the traditional range is still the most reliable place to start.

## How to judge

Taste is the test. A fast shot that tastes sour and thin is under extracted. A fast shot that tastes sweet and clear is doing its job.

documents.title: Forum thread: is a 40 second shot too long?
documents.text:
**Original post:** My shots take about 40 seconds to reach 36 grams from 18 grams in. Everything I read says 25 to 30 seconds, but honestly the coffee tastes fine to me, a bit heavy maybe. Should I grind coarser anyway?

**Reply 1:** If you like how it tastes, that is the only rule that matters. But "a bit heavy" might be the start of over extraction. Try one shot two steps coarser and compare them side by side.

**Reply 2:** What machine and how much pre-infusion? If your machine pre-infuses for 8 to 10 seconds, 40 seconds from the button might be completely normal.

**Original poster:** It does have pre-infusion, I think about 7 seconds before full pressure.

**Reply 2:** Then your shot is more like 33 seconds at full pressure. That is a bit long but not crazy.

**Reply 3:** Also depends on the roast. Very light roasts often taste better with longer shots and finer grinds. Dark roasts get harsh fast if they run long.

**Original poster:** It is a medium dark blend.

**Reply 3:** Then I would try coarser. Medium dark at 40 seconds often tastes heavy and a little bitter.

**Reply 4:** Check the spent puck too. A long shot from clumping or channeling is different from a long shot that is evenly ground. If the puck has holes, fix your prep before changing the grind.

**Original poster (update):** I went two steps coarser. The shot now takes 31 seconds including pre-infusion. It tastes lighter and sweeter, and I think I prefer it. The heavy feeling was probably the start of bitterness, like reply 1 said.

**Reply 5:** Good result. Most people do not notice mild over extraction until they taste a better shot next to it.

**Reply 6:** For the record, there is nothing magic about 25 to 30 seconds. It is a starting range that works for medium roasts, a 1:2 ratio and standard machines. Your update is a nice example of why it is a useful starting point, though.

**Original poster (final):** Thanks all. Lesson learned: compare two shots side by side before deciding something "tastes fine".

documents.title: Espresso shot time guide
documents.text:
How long should an espresso shot take? This espresso shot time guide will tell you about espresso shot time. Knowing the right espresso shot time is very important for making espresso.

Espresso is made by pushing hot water through coffee. The time this takes is called the shot time. The shot time can change how the espresso tastes. If the shot time is too short, the espresso might not taste right. If the shot time is too long, the espresso might not taste right either.

There are many things that can change the shot time. The coffee can change the shot time. The machine can change the shot time. The way you prepare the coffee can also change the shot time. That is why it is important to pay attention to the shot time.

Many people use a timer to measure the shot time. You can use a timer on your phone, or some machines have a timer built in. Using a timer is a good way to keep track of your shot time.

Some people say that there is a perfect shot time. Other people say that the perfect shot time depends on the coffee. We think that both of these ideas can be true. The important thing is that you enjoy your espresso.

If your espresso does not taste good, you can try changing the shot time. Try making the shot a little shorter or a little longer and see if it tastes better. Keep trying until you find the shot time you like best.

Remember that practice makes perfect. The more espresso you make, the better you will understand shot time. Do not worry if your first shots do not taste perfect. Everyone has to learn.

Thanks for reading this espresso shot time guide. We hope it helped you understand espresso shot time. Check out our other guides for more information about espresso.

Espresso shot time tips:
- Use a timer.
- Pay attention to the taste.
- Try different shot times.
- Practice a lot.
- Enjoy your espresso.

documents.title: A week of shot logs from a small café
documents.text:
Our café pulls about 250 shots a day on one machine. For one week, we logged every shot for the first hour of each morning to see how much shot time drifts and what we do about it. Here is what we found.

## The recipe

18 grams in, 38 grams out, house medium roast blend, timed from the button press. Our target range is 26 to 31 seconds.

## Daily summary (first hour of service)

| Day | Shots logged | Median time | Shortest | Longest | Grind changes made |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | 41 | 28 s | 23 s | 34 s | 2 |
| Tuesday | 38 | 29 s | 25 s | 33 s | 1 |
| Wednesday | 44 | 27 s | 21 s | 32 s | 3 |
| Thursday | 40 | 30 s | 26 s | 36 s | 2 |
| Friday | 47 | 28 s | 24 s | 33 s | 2 |
| Saturday | 52 | 29 s | 25 s | 35 s | 3 |
| Sunday | 35 | 28 s | 24 s | 31 s | 1 |

## What moved the shot time

- **Fresh bags.** On Wednesday we opened beans roasted four days earlier. The first shots ran fast, down to 21 seconds, until we ground finer twice.
- **Temperature of the grinder.** As the grinder warms up during service, shots slowly get faster. We usually make one small adjustment around the 30 minute mark.
- **Humidity.** Thursday was rainy and shots ran slower all morning.
- **Different baristas.** Distribution and tamping differences added a few seconds of spread, even with the same grind.

## What we learned

The median stayed within our range every day, but individual shots fell outside it about 15 percent of the time. Most of those were in the first ten minutes after opening or right after a new bag. We now pull two test shots before opening and after every new bag, and we taste them instead of trusting the clock alone.

## Does the time matter if the taste is fine?

We tasted 30 shots that fell outside our range. Shots under 24 seconds were mostly rated sour or thin. Shots over 33 seconds were rated heavy or bitter about half the time. Inside the range, almost every shot tasted good. For us, the range works as an early warning: a shot outside it is worth tasting before it goes to a customer.
